title: Master Xuanzang’s Work of Translating the Scriptures
excerpt: After returning to China, Master Xuanzang was held in high esteem by two successive emperors, Tang Taizong and Tang Gaozong, who supported him within the imperial palace and conferred upon him the title Tripitaka Master. Twice Tang Taizong urged him to abandon the monastic path and assist in governing, but the Master steadfastly declined, saying, “I would rather keep my vows in the black robes and propagate the Dharma left behind by the Buddha.” Tang Taizong then honored his wish and assisted his translation of the scriptures.

inline.s: returned to China and was held in high esteem by two successive emperors, Tang Taizong and Tang Gaozong, who supported him within the imperial palace and conferred upon him the title Tripitaka Master. Twice Tang Taizong urged him to abandon the monastic path and assist in governing, but the Master steadfastly declined, saying, “I would rather keep my vows in the black robes and propagate the Dharma the Buddha left behind.” Tang Taizong then honored his wish and assisted his sutra-translation work, establishing the sutra-translation academy at Chang’an and ordering the translation of new sutras.

After opening his translation bureau at Hongfu Monastery in Chang’an, Master Xuanzang asked the court to summon renowned monks from across the land who understood the Dharma and were skilled in writing to assist the work. Of these, twelve served as “verifiers of the text,” nine as “polishers of the phrasing”; other monks versed in philology served as “collators,” and monks proficient in Sanskrit served as “reciters of Sanskrit.” He also asked Tang Taizong to send scholars of letters to proofread and polish the texts. A complete translation bureau was thus formed at Hongfu Monastery, supplied by the court, which summoned more than twenty eminent monks from various regions to assist, each taking up such duties as verifying the meaning, polishing the phrasing, correcting the characters, and verifying the Sanskrit. Over nineteen years, they translated seventy-five works of sutras and treatises in 1,335 fascicles. The principal texts translated include: the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra in six hundred fascicles; the Sutra of the Great Bodhisattva Treasury in twenty fascicles; the Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Reception (the Tang translation of the Amitabha Sutra) in one fascicle; the Yogacarabhumi Sastra in one hundred fascicles; the Abhidharma Mahavibhasa Sastra in two hundred fascicles; the Abhidharma Nyayanusara Sastra in eighty fascicles; the Abhidharma Treatise on the Tenets in forty fascicles; the Sutra of the Five Paths in one fascicle; the Mahayana Mahasamnipata Sutra of the Ten Wheels of Ksitigarbha in ten fascicles; the Abhidharmakosa; the Cheng Weishi Lun (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) in ten fascicles; the Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only; the Mahayanasamgraha; the Mahayana Commentary on the Satasastra in ten fascicles; and the Mahayanasamgraha with the Commentary of Asvabhava in ten fascicles. Thus everything the Master had learned in India was transmitted to China.

Master Xuanzang studied in India for nineteen years, mastering the various doctrines of both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles and becoming proficient in Sanskrit as well as the various dialects and vernaculars of India. He once criticized the ancient sutra translators for their method of free, spontaneous translation based on the principle of “conveying the meaning,” and instead advocated a new rule of translation faithful to the original text and rendered word by word. Later generations of sutra translators took the standards Xuanzang established as their model, calling the sutras translated before Xuanzang the “old translations” and those translated after him the “new translations.” Xuanzang’s seriousness in translating the Buddhist sutras was unprecedented in history. His procedure was this: after translating a fascicle, he would first read the Sanskrit original aloud to the assembly, then read the Chinese draft. If anyone thought a passage was rendered inappropriately, the various experts would debate it back and forth until a conclusion was reached and it was universally agreed that the passage was beyond doubt; only then would they set about revising the translation and fixing it as final. Thus, in the sutras he corrected and translated, every sentence had been examined, weighed, and revised by experts, so that the sutras he translated matched the Sanskrit original in meaning, correct and without error.
From the Sui and Tang dynasties through the Northern Song, thanks to the government’s attention, the enterprise of translating the Buddhist scriptures achieved unprecedented development.
The Song Biographies of Eminent Monks divides the Tang sutra-translation organization into ten departments:

1. The Chief Translator. This was the central figure of the translation, who read aloud the Sanskrit original. The chief translator was usually the person with the greatest scholarly authority in the doctrine of the sutra being translated, though he was not necessarily involved in the linguistic work of translation. Moreover, they were mostly monks from India or the Western Regions whose mother tongue was not Chinese; some knew both languages, while some did not understand Chinese at all.

2. The Recorder. This was the work of transcribing the meaning of the Sanskrit into Chinese after the chief translator’s explanation. The recorder had to be proficient in both Sanskrit and Chinese; this was, in effect, the work of written translation.

3. The Interpreter. This post was established only when the chief translator did not understand Chinese, so that the Sanskrit he expounded could be thoroughly understood by the other translators. The interpreter was in effect the “tongue-man” — the work of oral interpretation.

4. The Verifier of Sanskrit. This was the office of checking whether the translated scripture matched the Sanskrit original. In practice, the Chinese translation was rendered back into Sanskrit and compared with the original.
5. The Polisher. This was the work of refining and polishing, so that the translated scripture, while its meaning remained unchanged, would be consistent in style and thus more elegant and dignified.

6. The Verifier of Meaning. The importance of translating the Buddhist scriptures into Chinese lies, after all, not only in matters of vocabulary and style; far more important is whether the doctrine is correct. Because this duty carried great weight, it was generally filled by several people.

7. The Chanting of Sanskrit. This was the Buddhist ceremony performed before and after the translation, used to compose the bearing and minds of the members of the translation bureau and to inspire them to arouse the bodhi mind of protecting the Dharma. It was an extremely important part of the translation work.
8. The Collator. This was the work of collating the translated scripture from the standpoint of Chinese philology. It was generally undertaken by a master of xiaoxue (traditional philology).

[Xiaoxue] “Xiaoxue” is the traditional name for the study of ancient language and writing, comprising three branches: phonology (the study of the sounds of characters), philology (the analysis of character forms), and exegetics (the explanation of character meanings).
9. The Overseer. This post was generally filled by a high official of the court. It was in effect a means of securing official recognition, a guardianship in name only.
10. The Verifier of Characters. This was not a standing post; Xuanying once held it. Its main duty was to select among rare and variant characters in Chinese.

[Xuanying] A monk of the Tang dynasty. He was learned and had a retentive memory, deeply versed in the study of phonology, writing, and exegetics. In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan reign (645 CE), after Xuanzang returned from the Western Regions and established his translation bureau, Xuanying also took part in the work of translating the scriptures. At the end of the Zhenguan reign, by imperial command he compiled the Sounds and Meanings of the Scriptures in twenty-five fascicles, known to the world as the Xuanying Yinyi. Later generations who studied the sounds and meanings of the scriptures all took it as their standard. His other works include the Commentary on the Mahayanasamgraha in ten fascicles, the Commentary on the Madhyantavibhaga, the Commentary on the Nyayapravesa in three fascicles, and the Sounds and Meanings of the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra in three fascicles.

The names of the posts in the Tang translation bureaus were, generally speaking, roughly as described. Yet they were not exactly the same in every bureau; there were perhaps some slight differences. Still, from this we can already see how complete the translation system of the ancient translation bureaus was. No wonder the modern scholar Zhang Jianmu, after comparing the surviving Sanskrit fragments of the Yogacarabhumi Sastra with Xuanzang’s translation, exclaimed: “I prostrate myself in admiration of how rigorous the Chinese translation is; few modern translations can come close to it.” With such a tightly organized translation bureau, and with a translation master like Xuanzang, it is hardly surprising that more than a thousand fascicles of scriptures and treatises have been handed down to us.
